subject: IRS
question: Examine the implication of belief in Prophets and enumerate the benefits therein.
modelAnswer:
Note: no category deals specifically with the articles of faith; 'Definition and Types of Tawhid' is used as the nearest.

Belief in the prophets and messengers (al-iman bir-rusul) is one of the six articles of faith (Q 2:285; 4:136). Muslims believe that Allah sent prophets to every nation (Q 16:36; 35:24), from Adam to Muhammad (SAW), the last (Khatam an-Nabiyyin, Q 33:40). Twenty-five are named in the Qur'an.

Implications:
1. A Muslim must believe in all the prophets without distinction (Q 2:285); rejecting one is rejecting all.
2. Prophets are human beings chosen by Allah, not divine. They are infallible (ma'sum) in conveying the message and of the highest character.
3. Their message is one: Tawhid and righteous living.
4. Muhammad (SAW) is the final prophet; no prophet comes after him, and his Shari'ah is binding until the end of time.
5. One must obey and follow the prophets' teachings; obedience to the Messenger is obedience to Allah (Q 4:80).
6. One must respect and love them, and invoke peace upon them.
7. Believers accept the revealed books brought by them (Tawrah, Zabur, Injil, Qur'an).

Benefits:
1. Guidance: knowledge of Allah, the purpose of life and the right way of worship, which reason alone could not fully discover.
2. Role models: their lives are practical examples of patience, honesty, justice and piety (Q 33:21).
3. Unity of humanity and religions: recognising all prophets promotes respect for other faiths (Jews and Christians).
4. Completion of faith, which leads to salvation in the Hereafter.
5. Moral and social reform: their teachings establish justice, brotherhood and good conduct.
6. Hujjah (proof): Allah does not punish a people before sending a messenger (Q 17:15), so people have no excuse.
7. Comfort and strength: their stories encourage believers in times of trial.
8. Knowledge of the unseen (ghayb), Paradise and Hell, angels and the Day of Judgement.

subject: IRS
question: State the distinctive features of Allah (SWT)
modelAnswer:
1. Oneness (Wahdaniyyah): Allah is One, without partner (Q 112:1).
2. Eternal and self-sufficient (as-Samad): He needs nothing, and all depend on Him (Q 112:2).
3. He neither begets nor is begotten (Q 112:3).
4. Nothing is like Him (Mukhalafah lil-hawadith): 'There is nothing like unto Him' (Q 42:11; 112:4).
5. The First and the Last (al-Awwal, al-Akhir): without beginning or end (Q 57:3).
6. Ever-Living, Self-Subsisting (al-Hayy al-Qayyum), who neither slumbers nor sleeps (Q 2:255, Ayat al-Kursi).
7. Creator, Sustainer and Owner of all (al-Khaliq, ar-Razzaq, al-Malik).
8. All-Knowing (al-'Alim): He knows the seen and the unseen (Q 6:59).
9. All-Powerful (al-Qadir): He has power over all things.
10. All-Hearing and All-Seeing (as-Sami', al-Basir).
11. Most Merciful and Most Gracious (ar-Rahman, ar-Rahim).
12. Just (al-'Adl) and the Judge on the Day of Judgement.
13. Will (Iradah): whatever He wills happens.
14. He alone deserves worship.
15. He has the Most Beautiful Names (al-Asma' al-Husna) (Q 7:180; 59:22–24).
16. He cannot be seen in this world (Q 6:103), and He is not limited by time or space.

subject: IRS
question: Examine the differences between an-Nabi and ar-Rasul.
modelAnswer:
Note: no category deals specifically with prophethood; 'Definition and Types of Tawhid' is used as the nearest.

An-Nabi (prophet) is one who receives revelation (wahy) from Allah. Ar-Rasul (messenger) is one who receives revelation and is commanded to convey a message, usually with a new law or book, to a people.

Differences (as generally explained by scholars):
1. Mission: a Nabi receives revelation and may teach and follow an existing law; a Rasul is commanded to deliver a message to a people.
2. Book/law: a Rasul usually brings a new Shari'ah or scripture (e.g. Musa – Tawrah, Dawud – Zabur, 'Isa – Injil, Muhammad – Qur'an); a Nabi generally follows and revives the law of a previous messenger (e.g. the prophets of Bani Isra'il who followed the Torah).
3. Scope: every Rasul is a Nabi, but not every Nabi is a Rasul. Rasul is the higher rank.
4. Number: prophets are more numerous (a hadith mentions about 124,000 prophets and 313–315 messengers, though scholars discuss its authenticity).
5. Audience: a Rasul is often sent to a people who rejected Allah, to bring a new message; a Nabi often works among believers.
6. Examples: Muhammad, Musa, 'Isa, Ibrahim and Nuh were both Rasul and Nabi; prophets such as Harun, Zakariyya and Yahya are generally described as prophets.
Muhammad (SAW) is both Rasulullah and Khatam an-Nabiyyin (the Seal of the Prophets) (Q 33:40).

subject: IRS
question: State the distinctive features of Propht Muhammad (SAW) among other Prophets (A.S).
modelAnswer:
Note: "Propht" is a misprint for Prophet.

1. Seal of the Prophets (Khatam an-Nabiyyin): no prophet comes after him (Q 33:40).
2. Universal messenger: sent to all mankind and jinn, not to one people only (Q 34:28; 7:158); earlier prophets were sent to their own nations.
3. Mercy to the worlds (Rahmatan lil-'alamin) (Q 21:107).
4. Recipient of the Qur'an, the final revelation, which is preserved from corruption and is his lasting miracle (Q 15:9).
5. His Shari'ah abrogates earlier laws and is valid for all times and places.
6. Al-Isra' wal-Mi'raj: the night journey to Jerusalem and the ascension to the heavens.
7. The excellent model (uswatun hasanah) in every area of life (Q 33:21), and the most detailed recorded life (Sirah and Hadith).
8. The great intercession (ash-Shafa'ah al-'Uzma) on the Day of Judgement, and al-Kawthar.
9. He was given special privileges (hadith of Jabir): help through awe (ru'b) cast in the hearts of enemies a month's distance away; the whole earth made a place of prayer and purification; spoils of war made lawful; intercession; and being sent to all people.
10. Leader of the prophets: he led them in prayer in Jerusalem during al-Isra'.
11. His name is joined with Allah's in the testimony of faith (shahadah) and the adhan.
12. His wives are 'mothers of the believers' (Q 33:6).

subject: IRS
category: Islamic Marriage and Divorce and Comparison with Marriage and Divorce Practices in Other Cultures
question: Examine the position of women in Islam.
modelAnswer:
Note: no category deals specifically with the status of women; the marriage and divorce category is used as the nearest.

Islam teaches that men and women are equal in human dignity and spiritual worth, with complementary roles and responsibilities.
1. Spiritual equality: both are created from a single soul (Q 4:1), and both receive equal reward for good deeds (Q 3:195; 33:35; 16:97).
2. Right to life: Islam abolished the pre-Islamic practice of burying baby girls alive (Q 81:8–9; 16:58–59).
3. Right to education: 'Seeking knowledge is an obligation on every Muslim', male and female. The Prophet's wife 'A'ishah was a great scholar.
4. Rights in marriage: a woman's consent is required for marriage; she is entitled to the dowry (mahr), which is her property (Q 4:4); the husband must provide maintenance (nafaqah), housing and kind treatment (Q 4:19); she may seek divorce (khul').
5. Economic rights: she can own, inherit (Q 4:7, 11), earn, trade and manage property in her own name, and is not obliged to spend it on the family.
6. Honour as mother: 'Paradise lies at the feet of mothers'; the Prophet named the mother three times before the father as most deserving of good companionship.
7. Protection and dignity: modest dress and conduct (Q 24:31; 33:59) protect her dignity; false accusation of chastity is severely punished (Q 24:4).
8. Social and political participation: women gave bay'ah to the Prophet (Q 60:12), took part in public affairs, and were consulted (e.g. Umm Salamah at Hudaybiyyah).
9. Kind treatment: 'The best of you are those who are best to their wives' (hadith, at-Tirmidhi).

Differences in roles: the man is the maintainer and protector of the family (qawwamun, Q 4:34); in inheritance a son's share is twice a daughter's (Q 4:11), balanced by the man's financial obligations; and some rules differ (e.g. testimony in financial contracts, Q 2:282). Muslims explain these as complementary roles rather than inferiority.
Note: the practice in some Muslim societies does not always reflect these teachings, because of local customs.

subject: IRS
question: Analize the procedure of Islam in establishing peaceful co-eficience among people.
modelAnswer:
Note: "co-eficience" is a misprint for co-existence.

Islam lays down principles and procedures for peaceful co-existence among people of different faiths, tribes and races:
1. Common origin of humanity: all people come from one male and one female and are made into nations and tribes 'that you may know one another'; the best is the most God-conscious (Q 49:13).
2. Freedom of religion: 'There is no compulsion in religion' (Q 2:256); 'To you your religion and to me mine' (Q 109:6).
3. Kindness and justice to peaceful non-Muslims: Allah does not forbid kindness and justice towards those who do not fight Muslims (Q 60:8).
4. Respect for the People of the Book (Jews and Christians): dialogue on common ground (Q 3:64); Muslims may eat their food and marry their chaste women (Q 5:5).
5. Treaties and covenants: the Constitution (Charter) of Madinah guaranteed rights for Muslims, Jews and other groups as one community (ummah) with mutual defence. The Treaty of Hudaybiyyah shows the value of peace agreements. Covenants must be fulfilled (Q 5:1; 17:34).
6. Protection of the dhimmi (protected non-Muslims) under Islamic rule: security of life, property and worship in return for jizyah. The Prophet warned against harming them.
7. Sanctity of life and property: killing one innocent soul is like killing all mankind (Q 5:32).
8. Justice for all, even towards enemies (Q 5:8).
9. Good neighbourliness: the Prophet stressed the rights of neighbours, whatever their religion.
10. Good conduct and wise preaching (da'wah) with beautiful exhortation and courteous argument (Q 16:125), and not insulting what others worship (Q 6:108).
11. Peace preferred: 'if they incline to peace, incline to it as well' (Q 8:61). Fighting is permitted only in self-defence and against oppression, within strict limits (Q 2:190).
12. Reconciliation (islah) between disputing parties (Q 49:9–10).

subject: IRS
category: The Regulations Governing Zakat and Sadaqah
question: Evaluate the differences between capitalism and Islam.
modelAnswer:
Note: no category deals specifically with economic systems; 'The Regulations Governing Zakat and Sadaqah' is used as the nearest.

Capitalism is an economic system based on private ownership of the means of production, the profit motive and free markets, with minimal government interference. The Islamic economic system is based on the Shari'ah, which recognises private property and markets but places them under moral and religious rules.

Differences:
1. Ownership: in capitalism the individual is the absolute owner of property. In Islam, absolute ownership belongs to Allah (Q 57:7), and humans are trustees (khalifah) who must use wealth according to His rules.
2. Interest: capitalism is built on interest-based banking and credit. Islam prohibits riba (usury/interest) (Q 2:275–279) and promotes profit-and-loss sharing (mudarabah, musharakah).
3. Motive: capitalism is driven mainly by the profit motive and self-interest. Islam allows profit but within ethical limits, aiming at the pleasure of Allah and the welfare of society (falah).
4. Distribution of wealth: capitalism allows unlimited accumulation, leading to wide inequality. Islam ensures redistribution through compulsory zakat, sadaqah, inheritance laws (which spread wealth among heirs) and the prohibition of hoarding (Q 9:34), 'so that wealth does not circulate only among the rich' (Q 59:7).
5. Lawful and unlawful (halal and haram): capitalism produces whatever is profitable. Islam forbids trade in haram goods and services (alcohol, pork, gambling, prostitution) and practices such as gharar (excessive uncertainty), fraud, monopoly hoarding (ihtikar) and cheating in measures.
6. Morality: capitalism separates economics from religion. In Islam, economic activity is an act of worship governed by ethics (honesty, fairness, mercy).
7. Role of the state: minimal in capitalism (laissez-faire). In Islam, the state has a duty to ensure justice, collect zakat, prevent exploitation and care for the needy (bayt al-mal).
8. Social security: capitalism leaves welfare largely to market forces. Islam makes care for the poor, orphans and needy a religious obligation.
9. Labour: Islam demands that workers be paid fairly and promptly ('before their sweat dries'), whereas pure capitalism lets wages be set by the market.
Similarities (brief): both recognise private property, trade, markets and lawful profit.

subject: IRS
question: State the biography of Shehu Usman Danfodio as Mijaddid of 18th century in Hausa land.
modelAnswer:
Note: "Mijaddid" is a misprint for Mujaddid (reformer/renewer).

Biography:
1. Birth: Shaykh 'Uthman ibn Fudi (Usman dan Fodio) was born in 1754 at Maratta in the Hausa state of Gobir, into the Toronkawa Fulani clan, a family of Islamic scholars. His father was Muhammad Fodio ('Fodio' means 'learned').
2. Education: he learnt the Qur'an from his father and studied under many scholars, especially Shaykh Jibril ibn 'Umar of Agades, who greatly influenced his reformist ideas. He studied tafsir, hadith, fiqh, Arabic and Sufism (Qadiriyyah order).
3. Preaching (from about 1774): he travelled across Gobir, Zamfara, Kebbi and other areas, preaching against bid'ah (innovation), syncretism (mixing Islam with traditional practices), corruption, illegal taxes, oppression by Hausa rulers and the neglect of women's education. He wrote many books in Arabic, Fulfulde and Hausa (e.g. Ihya' as-Sunnah, Bayan Wujub al-Hijrah, Kitab al-Farq).
4. Conflict with Gobir: his growing community (jama'a) alarmed the rulers of Gobir. Sultan Nafata restricted his activities (forbidding preaching except by him and forbidding conversion and the wearing of turbans and veils), and Sultan Yunfa tried to kill him.
5. Hijrah and Jihad: in 1804 he migrated (hijrah) to Gudu, where his followers elected him Amir al-Mu'minin (Commander of the Faithful). He declared jihad, defeating Gobir at Tabkin Kwotto (1804), and Alkalawa fell in 1808.
6. Sokoto Caliphate: the jihad spread across Hausaland and beyond, establishing the Sokoto Caliphate (founded around 1809), with emirates ruled by flag-bearers. He divided the administration between his son Muhammad Bello (Sokoto, east) and his brother Abdullahi (Gwandu, west).
7. Later life and death: he withdrew to scholarship and teaching, and died in 1817 at Sokoto.

Why he is regarded as a Mujaddid (reformer) of his age:
• He revived pure Islam according to the Qur'an and Sunnah and fought syncretism and innovation.
• He established a state based on the Shari'ah, with justice and an Islamic system of taxation and administration.
• He promoted education for men and women (his daughter Nana Asma'u was a famous scholar).
• He unified Hausaland politically and spread Islam widely in the region.
• He left a large body of scholarly writings.
Note: the jihad began in 1804, so his reform movement spans the late 18th and early 19th centuries.
